questions.stem: A 45-year-old male received a heart transplant one month ago. He develops a new supraventricular tachyarrhythmia without hypotension during a gastroscopy. The most appropriate therapy is

opts.why: Adenosine sensitivity is increased after transplantation; conventional doses can cause prolonged AV nodal block.

opts.why: Amiodarone has a long tissue half-life and interacts with immunosuppression; not the preferred immediate stable-rate-control choice.

opts.why: Short-acting IV beta blockade permits cautious titration in a stable patient; investigate for rejection.

opts.t: Verapamil as first choice regardless of immunosuppression
opts.why: Verapamil can interact with tacrolimus/ciclosporin and impair haemodynamics or cause bradycardia.

questions.expl: The repeatedly recalled 2022.2 exam answer was esmolol. In stable atrial tachyarrhythmia early after heart transplantation, cautious short-acting beta-blockade can provide rate control; assessment for graft rejection and review of immunosuppressant interactions are essential. Adenosine can cause prolonged AV block in the denervated heart and, if used, requires markedly reduced doses and monitoring. Verapamil/diltiazem may interact with calcineurin inhibitors. Amiodarone can cause bradycardia and prolonged drug interactions, making it less attractive as routine first-line treatment in the first post-transplant month.
questions.note: Reconstructed from multiple matching Brainscape answer-option sets; management depends on the exact tachycardia mechanism, ECG and graft status.
